title: Is it possible to sign the Apple Silicon build, as `homebrew` made it mandatory recently
body:
As of Oct 18th, the `homebrew` cask for Alacritty is marked as deprecated with a deadline of 2026-09-01 when it’s not signed the official way.

My question, therefore, is: Can the Apple Silicon build be signed to pass the `homebrew` requirements?

```shell
→ brew info alacritty
==> alacritty: 0.16.1
https://github.com/alacritty/alacritty/
Deprecated because it does not pass the macOS Gatekeeper check! It will be disabled on 2026-09-01.

→ brew doctor
Please note that these warnings are just used to help the Homebrew maintainers
with debugging if you file an issue. If everything you use Homebrew for is
working fine: please don't worry or file an issue; just ignore this. Thanks!

Warning: Some installed casks are deprecated or disabled.
You should find replacements for the following casks:
  alacritty
```

References:

- https://github.com/Homebrew/homebrew-cask/commit/8bde4810c028a9e530f1679f00db6089121ac21b
- https://github.com/orgs/Homebrew/discussions/6482

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
I do wonder if homebrew, a main package distributor, for macOS can sign things themselves for software they distribute. They also can fine tune packages to match e.g. macOS version, etc, etc.

Like open source projects paying 99$ to apple is not a great thing, howebrew on the other side, can pay 99$ and distribute tons of projects for those 99$ (I think that's fine?). And thus saving all of those open source projects a lot of money and also nerves.

Maybe I don't understand something here, but I was always curious, why package manager can not do things like that? mac ports IIRC can handle stuff like that.

It's a year before that anyway, so maybe something will change.

> I do wonder if homebrew, a main package distributor, for macOS can sign things themselves for software they distribute. They also can fine tune packages to match e.g. macOS version, etc, etc.

It seems Homebrew is being pretty hardline about this and that's really fucking lame.

As for changing it from a cask to allow users of Homebrew to build it themselves and self-sign, they explicitly don't accept that: https://docs.brew.sh/Acceptable-Formulae#stuff-that-builds-an-app

Best we can do is say, fuck Homebrew and if users want to download the application they'll have to download from our releases DMG and remove the quarantine themselves. Or build it from source themselves.

**Anyway, back when this was coming down the pipe, I wrote up an explanation on code signing and how this impact us here: https://participant2.com/ramblings/2021-02-02-signing-and-notarizing. Now that Homebrew doesn't help, you should read this for more info on your options.** I may update it to note the change with Homebrew, since it was at one point actually helping users use software.

> 
> Kchibisov is talking about gpg signatures, the de-facto standard for signing releases. With these signatures you get all the authenticity benefits, you just don't have to pay Apple anything.

I assumed he was referring to this:

https://github.com/alacritty/alacritty/blob/bf68154f9e4b91e5ba21dfb8151dbde23c46d47d/Makefile#L60

Signing the code is one thing, but it doesn't carry over to the built software, and has nothing to do with the way macOS runs applications.

In a better world than we live in, the GPG code signature chain would inform the application signature and the whole process would be derived from the source. But that's not the world we live in.

Signed commits are great if you build yourself though, which is basically the best solution as I've mentioned before in multiple places.

comments.author: participant5
comments.body:
> That's the problem, homebrew can certainly distribute software and save people a lot of money (99$ per project, since only homebrew need to apply for cert). 

I don't understand the logic behind saying Homebrew should pay for an Apple Developer account and then sign binaries for thousands of third-party projects. The trust implications of that model are mind-boggling, and it’s exactly the kind of thing that would get an Apple Developer account revoked immediately.

Homebrew doesn't have an Apple Developer account. The `.pkg` installer that installs `brew` is signed with my personal Apple Developer account, which I pay for out of pocket with money from my day job. Homebrew is a project run entirely by unpaid volunteers, and using my own account was simply a choice I made to make installation smoother for our users. I'm certainly not going to burn my account signing arbitrary third-party projects.

> it's also way better for security anyway, since package manager job is to shield against potentially unsafe software by people actually checking things.

I can't speak for other projects, but that is not Homebrew's job. We don't vet every single package for malware or implicitly trust anything. One of the reasons casks that fail Gatekeeper checks are deprecated in Homebrew/cask is to rely on Apple’s notarization and Gatekeeper, which is where that verification belongs.


> IIRC the same problem is not only with casks in some cases with homebrew, but solving the problem for everyone is not a way homebrew want to follow, I guess.

I'm not sure what this is supposed to mean, but it comes across as disingenuous and trivializes the complexity involved.

comments.author: participant3

> I don't understand the logic behind saying Homebrew should pay for an Apple Developer account and then sign binaries for thousands of third-party projects. The trust implications of that model are mind-boggling, and it’s exactly the kind of thing that would get an Apple Developer account revoked immediately.

That's exactly how package management works on Linux. comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
> I don't understand the logic behind saying Homebrew should pay for an Apple Developer account and then sign binaries for thousands of third-party projects. The trust implications of that model are mind-boggling, and it’s exactly the kind of thing that would get an Apple Developer account revoked immediately.

While you are most likely correct that this would lead to your Apple account being revoked, and that the trust model is difficult. That to me illustrates the problem with this entire setup, not a failure on our part. Forcing open source developers to pay Apple because that is what grants trust is wrong. What stops me from buying an Apple gift card, adding it to a throwaway account and paying that way. Are they really going to subpoena the store I bought the card at for video surveillance and track me down like that? Do you really want to live in a world where Apple is in charge of determining what software you're allowed to distribute and run?

In reality, Apple does minimal malware detection and only reacts if something is noticed. Which isn't very reassuring to the people who are affected by malware. The whole thing is security theater mostly, and users should instead be looking at the developers and ideally trusting someone who actually knows something about the source. Open source software is different from closed source, because it's readily auditable, but even closed source software should be signed off on. That is the idea behind notarization, but in practice it limits freedom to use the computer for people for somewhat limited security gains.

I stand by my position that Apple should focus it's energy on making their OS secure from technical exploits via strong process isolation and security features to hide sensitive information, and not universally limit free software.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
My intention was not to blame the authors or open source software in general. I respect the decision to not signing the app with an Apple signature.

What I do now instead, is the following.

_Install `rustup` and configure it_

```shell
brew install rustup
rustup-init
rustup default stable
rustc --version
```

_Install other dependencies (cmake, scdoc)_

```shell
brew install cmake scdoc
```

_Build_

```shell
git clone https://github.com/alacritty/alacritty.git
cd alacritty
make app
cp -r target/release/osx/Alacritty.app /Applications/
```

_Patch icon with [this custom one](https://yoolk.ninja/icons/alacritty/)_

```shell
brew install fileicon
fileicon set /Applications/Alacritty.app alacritty.icns
```

> _Part about quarantine bit was removed, as it will not be set anyway._
